rules.quote: Write amounts using the relevant currency symbol followed by numerals. Don’t put a space between the currency symbol and the numerals.

examples.note: Cents symbol 'c' directly follows numerals without space or full stop.

rules.quote: Use the letter ‘c’ for cents after the numerals.
rules.violation_condition: an amount expressed in cents written with a space between the numerals and 'c', or followed by an unnecessary full stop not ending a sentence
when: When writing an amount of less than $1 as a whole number of cents.
A full stop is permitted after the 'c' if it occurs at the end of a sentence.
rules.why: G-2: Consolidates formatting requirements for the cents suffix into one rule.

rules.quote: If the amount is a decimal number, always use 2 digits after the decimal point.
rules.violation_condition: a currency amount written in decimal form with fewer or more than 2 digits after the decimal point (e.g. $0.4 instead of $0.40 or $0.04)
when: If the amount is less than 10 cents, use a zero before the number of cents (e.g. $0.04).

covers.quote: Where content is clearly only referencing Australian dollars, use ‘$’.

examples.note: Australian dollars clearly understood from context.

parts.quote: The minimum wage in Australia is $19.49 per hour.

examples.note: A$ used without space for international audience.

parts.quote: The minimum wage in Australia is A$19.49 per hour.

examples.note: A$ used to avoid confusion with Hong Kong dollars.

parts.quote: The journalist was paid A$89 per hour during her posting in Hong Kong.

rules.quote: If users could be confused about the currency being referenced, place ‘A’ before the ‘$’. Don’t insert a space between them.
rules.specification: Use 'A$' with no space whenever Australian dollars might be confused with other dollar currencies.
rules.violation_condition: Australian dollar amounts written with a space between 'A' and '$' (e.g. 'A $'), or written without 'A' where confusion is likely in an international context
when: Where content is clearly only referencing Australian dollars, use '$'.
rules.why: G-2: Rules on when to use '$' vs 'A$' and spacing between 'A' and '$'.

covers.quote: Avoid the use of non-Australian currency symbols where possible.
When referencing ‘dollar’ currencies, use a country prefix followed by the ‘$’ symbol – for example, A$, C$, NZ$, US$. If there is any chance of confusion, use the 3-letter IBAN codes.
Use the currency symbol only, for example ‘£’ for the British pound, if you have evidence that it is the best way to meet a user need.

examples.note: IBAN currency codes used consistently without spaces.

parts.quote: Vietnam – VND4.18 million per month (urban Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City).

rules.quote: Use the 3-letter International Bank Account Number (IBAN) currency codes – for example, THB, USD, VND. This is the preferred method because it doesn’t use symbols and makes content more accessible.
rules.specification: Prefer 3-letter currency codes (e.g. USD, EUR) over symbols unless user research demonstrates symbols meet user needs.
rules.violation_condition: using non-Australian currency symbols where IBAN currency codes should be used
when: When referencing 'dollar' currencies, a country prefix followed by '$' (e.g. US$) may be used if no confusion.
Currency symbols alone (e.g. £) may be used if there is evidence it meets user needs.
rules.why: G-1, G-2: Consolidates the preference for 3-letter currency codes over foreign currency symbols.

examples.note: IBAN code followed immediately by numerals without a space.

rules.quote: Don’t place a space between the IBAN currency code and the numerals.
rules.violation_condition: a space between a 3-letter currency code and the numerals (e.g. 'AUD 19.49')
rules.why: G-2: Specific typographic rule on spacing for currency codes.

examples.note: Consistent 2 decimal places across all listed currencies.

rules.quote: Use the same number of decimal places for all the currencies you refer to.
rules.specification: Within a block or list comparing multiple currencies, maintain identical decimal precision across all items.
rules.violation_condition: inconsistent number of decimal places across currency figures in the same context/list
rules.why: G-2: Self-contained formatting rule across related currency amounts.

rules.quote: Don’t also use the IBAN currency code.
rules.violation_condition: using both a currency symbol and an IBAN currency code for the same amount (e.g. '$7.25 USD' or 'USD $7.25')
when: When using foreign or Australian currency symbols.
rules.why: G-2: Redundant specification of symbol plus code.

examples.note: Japanese yen (¥) explained on first use.

examples.note: US$ is widely known, so no explanation needed on first use.

parts.quote: The minimum wage in the United States is currently US$7.25 per hour.

rules.quote: Explain them on first use unless they are very widely known (for example, US$).
rules.specification: Provide the full currency name (e.g. Japanese yen (¥)) on first reference when using less common currency symbols.
rules.violation_condition: a foreign currency symbol used without explanation on first mention, unless it is widely known (such as US$)
when: Widely known symbols such as US$ do not require explanation.
rules.why: G-2: Standalone document-level accessibility rule for unfamiliar currency symbols.

covers.quote: Few people would recognise these symbols now, so write them out in full.
Some countries still use pounds as their currency. If there is any chance of confusion, state ‘former Australian pounds’ or use the symbol ‘A£’.

rules.quote: Use words rather than symbols for former Australian currency.

when: If there is any chance of confusion with other countries using pounds, state 'former Australian pounds' or use 'A£'.
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Covers historical Australian currency unit rules.
